newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria defiant against EU on anonymous accounts.
newsitem.headline: Austria defiant against EU on anonymous accounts.

text.p: Austrian Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger remained defiant over the nation's controversial anonymous savings accounts and said he was not afraid of threatened legal action by the European Union.
"If necessary we will go before the European Court of Justice. We must not be afraid to do so," Edlinger told Austrian television late on Friday night.
Edlinger was speaking in response to a nine-page letter sent to the Austrian government by the European Commission calling for the abolition of anonymous savings accounts.
Austria has two months to justify its position to the Commission. If it fails to provide a satisfactory response the nation could be taken to the European Court of Justice.
Critics of Austrian banking say anonymous savings and securities accounts offer an open door to money launderers.
"I believe Austria fulfils the EU guidelines against money laundering," Edlinger said. "The cause of this discussion is not anonymity but EU measures against money laundering."

The letter, signed by EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti, demands that Austria identify all anonymous bank accounts -- believed to number around 26 million in a nation of seven million inhabitants.
The government and the central bank say the accounts, which have a 200-year tradition, are a key part of the savings culture.
Edlinger said he thought Austria could win the battle in court, but admitted he could not guarantee the future existence of the accounts.
In August, when the government outlawed new securities accounts, existing accounts contained an estimated 400 billion schillings, of which 60 billion was owned by foreigners.
